title: Women + AI Summit, Real Talk: Leadership, Learning, and Not Letting “The Trap” Write Your Story
author: Marlene Gebauer · Nicole Morris · Sabra Tomb · Adele Shen · Chanal Neves McClain · Dyane O'Leary · Stephanie Everett

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: Wilkins shifts the focus from practitioner-led experimentation and shared, reliability-conscious implementation to identifying AI-centred law firms as a distinct emerging business model. Her launch count and delivery-model distinction support the cluster’s narrower forecast of service-model expansion, but do not address its principal proposition that redesign should proceed through practitioner engagement before technological certainty.
qs: Since late 2024, we’ve seen 15 to 20 firms launch globally.
And the commonality of all of them is that they place AI at the center of their legal service delivery.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: The source evaluates conference design and participant engagement, not whether legal AI benefits depend on organisational adaptation, human control, workforce preparation or pricing changes. It therefore provides insufficient evidence to determine a position on the cluster proposition.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: The source accepts continuous learning as a practical capability and materially develops the cluster’s approach by proposing two concrete methods: framing AI education through legal reasoning rather than interface operation, and using collaborative workshops to build and spread practical knowledge. Its claims remain practitioner recommendations and activity descriptions rather than measured learning outcomes.
qs: Use the tools, but when you talk about them, it’s from lawyering concepts, not “how to use the tool.”  Marlene Gebauer 31:06  Yes.
It was coming up with practical ways to build AI knowledge, and then spread knowledge and use.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source accepts the need for AI-enabled training while materially developing the cluster’s proposed approach: it integrates tool use with judgment, ethics and client counseling, and provides a concrete low-stakes simulated-client exercise. It appropriately presents these as teaching practices rather than measured learning outcomes.
qs: My exercise had students work with actual AI tools, but then only discuss them through the lens of traditional lawyering skills like judgment and ethics and critical thought, to shape students so they weren’t just using a tool.

They were able to, in a low-stakes environment, see what it’s like to prepare for and come up with some kind of strategy for client counseling, and to have real-time dynamic responses, because the models are capable of doing some helpful things in the classroom.

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: The source extends the cluster’s market-maturity account by identifying AI-centred law firms as an emerging service-delivery model and providing Pierson Ferdinand’s partner-only structure as a concrete example. It also treats disruption as a question for investigation rather than demonstrating superior performance or client outcomes, consistent with the cluster’s evidentiary caution.
qs: And the commonality of all of them is that they place AI at the center of their legal service delivery.
and their model is a partner-only law firm with no associates, but they really have built from the ground up a tech stack and a way of delivering legal services with AI at its core.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that AI should selectively absorb routine work within human-led practice, freeing people for strategy and leadership. It materially extends the proposition with concrete adoption requirements: explaining limitations, integrating AI into workflows, and using practice-specific, peer-supported training.
qs: Using AI has allowed me to focus on strategy and vision versus being overwhelmed with day-to-day tasks.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s cautious distinction between product or business-model expansion and demonstrated value. It documents an AI-centred, partner-only delivery model but frames its actual disruptive effect as an open question requiring further investigation, rather than as an established outcome.
qs: and their model is a partner-only law firm with no associates, but they really have built from the ground up a tech stack and a way of delivering legal services with AI at its core.
We’re really trying to dig into if and how these firms are disrupting the way we’ve seen law delivered and practiced in the past before.

kp.k: AI-centered firms represent a distinct legal delivery model
kp.d: Stephanie Wilkins reports that 15 to 20 firms launched globally since late 2024 under AI firm, AI-first or AI-native labels. She distinguishes businesses built around AI-centered legal service delivery from traditional firms with strong AI functions or committees. She characterizes this as a disruptive business model, while describing investigation of whether and how disruption occurs rather than presenting demonstrated market effects.
qs: Since late 2024, we’ve seen 15 to 20 firms launch globally.
And the commonality of all of them is that they place AI at the center of their legal service delivery.
But we’re talking about firms that are not just a traditional law firm with a particularly robust AI function or an AI committee.
We’re really trying to dig into if and how these firms are disrupting the way we’ve seen law delivered and practiced in the past before.

kp.k: Pierson Ferdinand illustrates partner-only, AI-centered delivery
kp.d: Wilkins describes Pierson Ferdinand as launching in January 2024 with 130 founding partners and subsequently more than doubling in size. Its partner-only structure has no associates, alongside a technology stack built around AI delivery. This is a reported organizational example, not evidence that AI caused its growth or eliminated previously existing associate positions.
qs: Pierson Ferdinand, for those who aren’t familiar, launched about two years ago in January 2024 with 130 founding partners, and they’ve more than doubled in that size.
and their model is a partner-only law firm with no associates, but they really have built from the ground up a tech stack and a way of delivering legal services with AI at its core.

kp.k: Gendered AI narratives motivate collective learning
kp.d: Marlene Gebauer reports that Cat Moon organized the summit in response to a narrative that women use or participate in AI less than men, treating either actual underparticipation or a false narrative as problematic. Nicole Morris describes the gathering as bringing academics, law firms and vendors together to exchange workplace experiences, risks and concerns, and expand AI knowledge particularly among women. Neither establishes an actual gender adoption gap.
qs: It’s centered around the fact that there’s a narrative out there that women are not using AI as much as men, or are not involved in AI as much as men.
Her thought was, if this is real, it’s a problem. And if it’s a false narrative, it’s also a problem.

all convening to talk about how AI is being used in their workplace, how they see the tools as helpful, what are the risks and concerns they have, and then how do we expand AI knowledge, particularly to women, and how we can do more with it to increase our productivity.

kp.k: Reported competence penalties differ by gender
kp.d: Gebauer recounts summit statistics from software engineers evaluating identical code, with author gender and AI use disclosed experimentally. She reports competence penalties as 'Men, negative six. Women, negative 13' and a further 26% comparison involving male nonusers penalizing women. The transcript provides no study citation, sample size or units for the first figures, and its wording of the 26% statistic is ambiguous. These are reported cross-domain findings, not measurements of legal professionals.
qs: They talk about competence penalties of men who use AI and women who use AI. Men, negative six. Women, negative 13.
Then 26% of men who didn’t use AI themselves penalized women who did, 26% more harshly than they penalized other men for the same work.
This was software engineers evaluating identical code. They were only told whether it was written by a man or a woman, with or without AI.

kp.k: AI can release leadership capacity from routine tasks
kp.d: Sabra Tomb describes her personal experience of using AI to shift attention from day-to-day management toward strategy and vision. Gebauer interprets this as a leadership opportunity rather than simply a productivity gain, particularly for women pulled into administrative responsibilities, and extends the argument to leaders without sufficient people to delegate to. The evidence offered is experiential rather than a measured productivity or career-advancement result.
qs: Using AI has allowed me to focus on strategy and vision versus being overwhelmed with day-to-day tasks.
It wasn’t “AI is a productivity tool.” Instead, she framed it as allowing you to be a leader, and impacting your highest calling.
The trap is you start getting into leadership roles but keep being pulled into day-to-day tasks.
If you don’t have depth to delegate, if you don’t have other people to do it for you, the AI can do it for you.

kp.k: Adoption requires safety, peer learning and visible leadership
kp.d: Gebauer endorses a summit framework combining technical and learning safe spaces, peer learning, leadership support and internal AI evangelists. She explains technical safety in terms of governance and safe use. Greg Lambert argues from workplace experience that leaders must visibly use tools and share their experiences to encourage associates; both favor complementary top-down and bottom-up adoption rather than relying solely on junior enthusiasm.
qs: You need safe spaces, technical safe spaces and learning safe spaces. You need peer learning, learning from and with peers.
Leadership needs to support it and do it, and people need to see that happening.
Then you need the AI spark, who gets the ball rolling, who are your evangelists.
Governance, knowing what you’re doing. And being able to work on it in a safe way.
If an associate sees senior partners using it, they’re encouraged. If they don’t see usage from leadership, they’re not encouraged.

kp.k: Practical AI literacy extends beyond operating tools
kp.d: Gebauer identifies three priority capabilities: translating ideas into prompts, explaining benefits and limitations, and integrating AI into workflows. She argues that people using AI for clients should be comfortable discussing it, rather than leaving communication solely to AI specialists. Training recommendations include basic, governance and practice-related instruction, CLE, short sessions, peer demonstrations and social channels for sharing questions and experience. These are recommendations, not comparative training-effectiveness findings.
qs: Turning an idea into a prompt. Explaining pros and cons to someone, what it does and doesn’t do. Integrate it into workflows.
People using it for clients need to feel comfortable talking about it.
In-person training. Basic training. Governance training. Practice-related training. Offer CLE. Do short bites.
Peer training can be best because if a peer is doing it in a similar practice, you can see the relevance. That motivates you.
You learn from others’ questions and experiences, and it’s not a heavy lift.

kp.k: Legal education should integrate human and AI skills
kp.d: Suffolk professors Chanal Neves McClain and Dyane O’Leary argue against separating human lawyering skills from AI instruction into isolated modules. O’Leary describes students using actual AI tools but discussing them through judgment, ethics and critical thought. McClain argues that the capabilities must coexist so lawyers can lead technology adoption in education and the profession. The transcript describes instructional approaches without reporting assessed learning outcomes.
qs: Today we discussed how we don’t have to look at the human skills and the AI skills as bifurcated pathways.
we need both coexisting together at this time so that, as lawyers, we can lead how this technology will be adopted by our educational institutions and by our profession.
A lot of courses kind of stuff AI into a two-week module and then do away with it, or stuff human counseling into a two-week module and then do away with it.

My exercise had students work with actual AI tools, but then only discuss them through the lens of traditional lawyering skills like judgment and ethics and critical thought, to shape students so they weren’t just using a tool.

kp.k: AI client simulations support low-stakes counseling practice
kp.d: McClain describes building a video-chatting simulated client for students to counsel on a legal problem. Its dynamic responses allow practice in preparation and counseling strategy within a low-stakes classroom environment. The hosts see this as combining technology with human counseling skills, while Lambert separately endorses academic settings as a safe place to learn AI capabilities and limitations.
qs: I built a client, a video-chatting client, that students counseled on a legal problem.

They were able to, in a low-stakes environment, see what it’s like to prepare for and come up with some kind of strategy for client counseling, and to have real-time dynamic responses, because the models are capable of doing some helpful things in the classroom.
They learn what tools do and don’t do, blending human skills and AI.

kp.k: Expert backgrounds and incentives shape AI narratives
kp.d: Adele Shen describes a humorous classification of AI experts intended to reveal how their backgrounds inform biases. Gebauer reports the categories as technocratic oracles, extinction alarmists and touch grass humanists. The hosts criticize self-promotional certainty about AI’s future and urge skepticism toward commentators who make themselves the story. This is a qualitative interpretive framework, not an empirical classification or prediction.
qs: I used a little bit of humor to categorize them, to point out the specific background they have and how it might inform their biases.
She broke people into technocratic oracles, extinction alarmists, and touch grass humanists.
When talking heads become the story, red flags go up.
I don’t think anybody is omnipotent about what’s going to happen.

kp.k: Women should challenge limiting stories about AI participation
kp.d: Stephanie Everett uses a personal anecdote about internalizing predictions to argue that women can choose different stories about their futures and their use of AI to shape the profession. Gebauer applies this to discouraging narratives about who belongs in AI, emphasizing the danger of internalizing them. This is a motivational recommendation grounded in personal experience, not evidence that reframing narratives removes structural bias.
qs: I didn’t realize it, but I started internalizing that story and allowing it to live in the back of my head and make decisions about my life.
women coming together and talking about what we want our stories to be, how we are going to leverage AI, and how we are going to drive our profession forward.
My takeaway is, you don’t have to live the stories you’re told. You can question those stories.
The danger is listening, believing, internalizing.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: AI-centered law firms represent an emerging legal-service delivery model.
pts.d: Stephanie Wilkins describes AI-first and AI-native firms as a new model organized around AI in service delivery, rather than traditional firms with substantial AI functions. She characterizes the model as disruptive while also presenting its actual effects as a subject for investigation. Her example, Pierson Ferdinand, combines a partner-only structure with an AI-centered technology stack; she does not establish that AI caused its staffing structure or growth.

pts.k: AI can free capacity for strategy and leadership rather than only increasing task productivity.
pts.d: Sabra Tomb reports that AI helped her move from day-to-day management toward strategic work. This is a personal account of augmentation in a law-school leadership role, not a claim of autonomous legal-service delivery.

pts.k: Summit research presented a gender-differentiated competence penalty for AI use.
pts.d: Research statistics presented at the summit, relayed by Marlene Gebauer, concern software engineers evaluating identical code. The reported finding is harsher competence judgments for women using AI than for men. This is cross-domain evidence, not a measured effect among lawyers. The underlying researchers are not identified in the transcript, so the finding cannot be attributed more specifically.

pts.k: Visible leadership use and practice-relevant peer learning are said to encourage legal-workplace AI adoption.
pts.d: Greg Lambert makes the direct claim that leaders using AI and discussing their experience encourage associates to adopt it. Marlene Gebauer independently endorses peer training as motivational. These are the hosts' own substantive claims, distinct from findings they merely relay from other speakers.

pts.k: AI and human lawyering skills can be taught together, including through simulated client counseling.
pts.d: Chanal Neves McClain argues for integrated human and AI skills so lawyers can lead adoption. Dyane O’Leary describes examining AI use through judgment, ethics, and critical thought. McClain reports building a video-chatting simulated client that gives students dynamic counseling practice. These are educational applications, not claims that AI replaces professional judgment.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Wilkins offers an observed launch count and a named firm example, not comparative performance measurements.
pts.d: Wilkins reports 15–20 launches globally since late 2024 and describes Pierson Ferdinand's founding size and subsequent growth. Legal Technology Hub's planned interview series supplies the context. The transcript provides no counting methodology, quantified client outcomes, or evidence isolating AI's contribution to growth.

pts.k: The leadership benefit is supported by Tomb's personal experience.
pts.d: Tomb explicitly identifies her talk as experiential. No tools, time savings, controlled comparisons, or promotion outcomes are specified.

pts.k: The account describes identical-code evaluations but leaves important study details unspecified.
pts.d: Evaluators were told the author's gender and whether AI was used. The transcript supplies neither a study citation nor sample size or units for the negative-six and negative-13 figures. Its wording of the additional 26% statistic is ambiguous and is preserved rather than reconstructed.

pts.k: The adoption claims rely on workplace impressions and workshop discussion.
pts.d: Lambert refers to what he hears and emphasizes at work; Gebauer recounts training ideas discussed at the summit. Neither provides adoption rates or comparative evidence establishing which training method works best.

pts.k: The evidence consists of instructors' accounts of classroom exercises.
pts.d: O’Leary and McClain describe actual teaching activities. No measured learning gains, comparison groups, or longitudinal professional outcomes are supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The market claim concerns recent emergence, not a dated forecast of industry-wide replacement.
pts.d: Wilkins dates the observed wave to late 2024 onward. The source is labeled 2026. Her category requires AI at the core of delivery; merely having an AI committee or a robust AI function does not qualify. No deadline for broader disruption is offered.

pts.k: Tomb describes an already-experienced benefit, with no adoption period or future deadline.
pts.d: The benefit depends on using AI to reduce the burden of routine work. The transcript does not specify implementation duration or the range of tasks delegated.

pts.k: The study period is unstated; the finding concerns judgments under disclosed gender and AI-use conditions.
pts.d: These are reported study results presented at the summit, not a future prediction. No longitudinal persistence or legal-sector replication is claimed.

pts.k: Adoption benefits are presented as current and conditional on visible participation, relevance, and safe learning environments.
pts.d: The summit framework, as reported by Gebauer, calls for technical and learning safety, peer learning, leadership support, and people who initiate adoption. No timeline or quantified expected effect is supplied.

pts.k: The instructors describe present classroom capabilities under low-stakes, human-skills-oriented conditions.
pts.d: McClain says both skill sets need to coexist now. O’Leary contrasts integration with isolating AI or counseling in short modules. No forecast of future model capability is offered.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The examples concern boutiques, larger partner-only firms, and client-facing delivery.
pts.d: Wilkins identifies varied firm sizes and structures. Pierson Ferdinand illustrates delivery without associates, but she does not predict profession-wide associate displacement. The firms are described as law firms, not automatically as ALSPs or software vendors.

pts.k: The direct example is a woman leading training and business development in legal education.
pts.d: Tomb works at the University of Dayton School of Law as a director and professor. Her stated interest extends to empowering other women through AI, but the concrete outcome described is her own increased strategic focus.

pts.k: The direct subjects are perceived male and female code authors; the summit frames the issue as relevant to women's AI participation.
pts.d: The reported effect is a competence-evaluation penalty, not a measured difference in work quality or AI proficiency. The summit's motivating concern about women's participation is explicitly framed as a narrative whose truth is unresolved, rather than an established adoption gap.

pts.k: Senior partners, associates, and peers in similar practices are the identified adoption participants.
pts.d: Leadership acts as a visible example; associates receive encouragement; practitioners learn relevance from colleagues working in comparable contexts. This concerns uptake and literacy, not demonstrated improvements in client outcomes.

pts.k: First-year law students and legal educators gain new ways to practice and teach lawyering skills.
pts.d: Both instructors teach Suffolk's first-year legal practice skills class. Students practice counseling strategy and critical engagement with AI. The broader aspiration is lawyer-led adoption by educational institutions and the profession; improved outcomes for real clients are not measured.
